headline: Figma's AI Agent Lives on Canvas
subheadline: Figma just shipped an on-canvas AI design agent that works across Design, Make, and code — and it directly impacts your design system and MCP work. Plus: Brad Frost on agentic design systems, and Claude's latest enterprise moves.

sections.label: Trending
sections.title: Figma's built-in AI agent now lives on the canvas
sections.description: This is the big one. Figma launched a purpose-built AI agent that sits right on the canvas and in the left rail — it can explore ideas, make bulk edits, apply design systems, and turn feedback into action across Figma Design, Figma Make, and code. Given you're building a Figma MCP + Claude integration for your company's white-label sport apps, this could fundamentally change what your system needs to expose. Worth understanding what it can already do natively before you build around it.

sections.label: Read
sections.title: Figma AI in 2026: Everything it can do — and what it still can't
sections.description: An honest breakdown of where Figma AI actually delivers and where it falls short. This is useful for you specifically because knowing the gaps tells you exactly where your MCP + Claude integration adds value that Figma's native AI doesn't cover — especially around design tokens, component architecture, and white-label theming logic.

sections.label: Listen
sections.title: Agentic Design Systems in 2026 with Brad Frost
sections.description: Brad Frost talks about how autonomous agents are now assembling UIs using the same components your human designers use. This is directly relevant to your design system work — if agents are consumers of your component library, your tokens and architecture need to be legible to machines, not just humans. Perfect stroller listen. 🍼

sections.label: Read
sections.title: The Future of Enterprise Design Systems: 2026 Trends and Tools
sections.description: Supernova's take on how design systems are evolving from passive libraries to active, agentic workflows. They frame it around automation, scaling, and future-proofing — which maps directly to what you're building. Good strategic framing if you're thinking about pitching your MCP integration internally as more than just a tool.

sections.label: Concept of the day
sections.title: Agentic AI vs. Generative AI — and why it matters for product
sections.description: There's a useful distinction emerging: Generative AI writes a user story when asked. Agentic AI independently finds a bug, traces its root cause, and proposes a fix. For your evolving role toward product builder/leadership, this matters — the tools you're building with (Claude, MCP, Cursor) are shifting from 'assistants you prompt' to 'agents that act.' Understanding this framing helps you articulate what you're actually building.

sections.label: Did you know
sections.title: Figma MCP server demand is driving measurable business growth
sections.description: Quartz reports that Figma's MCP server adoption has been strong enough to signal upside for the company's valuation. This validates what you're already doing — MCP isn't a niche experiment anymore, it's becoming core infrastructure. Your early expertise here is genuinely ahead of the curve.

sections.label: Think about this
sections.title: If AI agents consume your design system, who are you really designing for?
sections.description: Brad Frost's talk and the Supernova piece both point to the same shift: your design system's primary consumer might soon be an AI agent, not a junior designer. What does that mean for how you name tokens, structure components, and write documentation? Your MCP work already touches this — but it might be worth making 'agent-legibility' an explicit design principle.
